hints: Compare the physical states on each side of reaction 1, count how many moles of solid, liquid and gas appear as reactants and as products.
walkthrough:
Picture disorder in each state**
Think of entropy as how spread out and disordered particles are. Solids are tightly packed and ordered with low entropy, liquids can move a little more, and gases spread freely with very high entropy. So any change that makes gas from solid is a big jump in disorder.

Count what you start and finish with**
Look at $\text{SiO}_2(\text{s}) + 2\text{C}(\text{s}) \rightarrow \text{Si}(\text{l}) + 2\text{CO}(\text{g})$. You start with 3 moles of ordered solid and no gas. You finish with 1 mole of liquid plus 2 moles of gas. You have created much more mobile, disordered particles, so entropy of the system increases.
Final answer: 3 mol of solid form 1 mol of liquid and 2 mol of gas, so disorder increases and $\Delta S$ is positive.

hints: Write down the Gibbs equation $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$ and note the signs of $\Delta H$ and $\Delta S$ for reaction 1.
Think about what happens to the size of the $T\Delta S$ term as $T$ gets larger, and what that does to the sign of $\Delta G$.
walkthrough:
Set up the Gibbs balance**
Feasibility is decided by $$\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$$ Here $\Delta H$ is large and positive (highly endothermic) which is unfavourable, but $\Delta S$ is positive from (a)(i) which is favourable. The two terms fight each other.

See why heating wins**
The favourable term is multiplied by $T$. As temperature rises, $T\Delta S$ gets bigger and eventually outweighs the positive $\Delta H$. Then $\Delta H - T\Delta S$ turns negative, so $\Delta G$ becomes negative and the reaction becomes feasible. That is why this extraction needs over $2000^{\circ}\text{C}$.
Final answer: As $T$ increases, $T\Delta S$ becomes larger and more positive. Since $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$, $\Delta G$ becomes more negative so the reaction becomes more feasible.

hints: Recall the rule $\Delta S^{\ominus} = \Sigma S^{\ominus}(\text{products}) - \Sigma S^{\ominus}(\text{reactants})$ and list the product and reactant values from Table 2.1.
Remember to multiply the $\text{HCl}(\text{g})$ entropy by 3 because reaction 2 uses 3 moles, then combine to find the final sign and units.
walkthrough:
Write the products minus reactants sum**
For $\text{Si}(\text{s}) + 3\text{HCl}(\text{g}) \rightarrow \text{SiHCl}_3(\text{g}) + \text{H}_2(\text{g})$: $$\Delta S^{\ominus} = [S^{\ominus}(\text{SiHCl}_3) + S^{\ominus}(\text{H}_2)] - [S^{\ominus}(\text{Si}) + 3 \times S^{\ominus}(\text{HCl})]$$ Never forget the 3 in front of $\text{HCl}$, that is the most common slip.

Substitute and calculate**
Put in the numbers: $$(314 + 131) - (19 + 3 \times 187) = 445 - (19 + 561) = 445 - 580 = -135 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{mol}^{-1}$$ The value is negative because 4 moles of gas with high entropy become only 2 moles of gas, so disorder falls.

hints: Reaction 3 is the reverse of reaction 2, so decide how $\Delta S^{\ominus}$ for reaction 3 relates to your answer in (b)(i).
At the point where feasibility just begins $\Delta G = 0$, so $T = \Delta H / \Delta S$. Check that $\Delta H$ is converted to $\text{J mol}^{-1}$ before dividing.
walkthrough:
Flip the entropy for the reverse reaction**
Reaction 3 is $\text{SiHCl}_3(\text{g}) + \text{H}_2(\text{g}) \rightarrow \text{Si}(\text{s}) + 3\text{HCl}(\text{g})$, exactly the opposite of reaction 2. So just change the sign: $$\Delta S^{\ominus}(\text{reaction 3}) = -\Delta S^{\ominus}(\text{reaction 2}) = -(-135) = +135 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{mol}^{-1}$$

Use the zero Gibbs boundary**
A reaction just becomes feasible when $$\Delta G = 0$$ so $$0 = \Delta H - T\Delta S$$ $$T = \frac{\Delta H}{\Delta S}$$ Convert $\Delta H = +219.3 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1} = +219300 \text{ J mol}^{-1}$ to match entropy units, then: $$T = \frac{219300}{135} = 1624 \text{ K}$$ Above this temperature $T\Delta S > \Delta H$ and $\Delta G$ is negative.

Final answer: For reaction 3, $\Delta S^{\ominus} = +135 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{mol}^{-1}$.
$T = \Delta H / \Delta S = 219.3 \times 10^{3} / 135 = 1624 \text{ K}$

hints: Use $n = m / M_r$ with $M_r$ of Si = 28.1 to find moles of Si, then use the half-equation $\text{SiO}_2 + 4e^{-} \rightarrow \text{Si} + 2\text{O}^{2-}$ to find moles of electrons needed.
Convert moles of electrons to charge with $Q = n(e^{-}) \times 96500$, then rearrange $Q = It$ to $t = Q / I$ with $I = 6.00 \text{ A}$.
walkthrough:
Link silicon to electrons**
First find silicon: $$n(\text{Si}) = \frac{1.00}{28.1} = 0.0356 \text{ mol}$$ The cathode equation $\text{SiO}_2 + 4e^{-} \rightarrow \text{Si} + 2\text{O}^{2-}$ tells you each Si needs 4 electrons, because Si goes from +4 in $\text{SiO}_2$ to 0 in Si. So: $$n(e^{-}) = 4 \times 0.0356 = 0.142 \text{ mol}$$

Turn electrons into time**
One mole of electrons carries 96500 C, so: $$Q = n(e^{-}) \times 96500 = 0.1424 \times 96500 = 13737 \text{ C}$$ Charge is current times time, $Q = It$, so: $$t = \frac{Q}{I} = \frac{13737}{6.00} = 2289 \text{ s}$$ That is about 38 minutes to deposit just 1.00 g, showing why 4 electrons per atom makes this energy intensive.

Final answer: Moles $\text{Si} = 1.00 / 28.1 = 0.0356 \text{ mol}$, moles $e^{-} = 4 \times 0.0356 = 0.142 \text{ mol}$.
$Q = 0.142 \times 96500 = 13737 \text{ C}$, $t = Q / I = 13737 / 6.00 = 2290 \text{ s}$ (2289 s with unrounded values).
